samples.summary: Identity change under a mounted editor rebinds the offline store scope to the newly signed-in account while the previous account's attached document is still live, so account A's content can be written into account B's store scope
samples.evidence: `inner` (the `DocumentProvider` subtree) is built once at line 301 and rendered as the SAME element object in both the durable and non-durable branches. When another tab signs A out and B in on a shared device, React Query refetches `['me','optional']`, `person` becomes B, `subject` (line ~264, `${person?.id ?? 'anon'}:${docKey}`) changes, and the held decision is re-made. React then reconciles `DurableYorkieProvider` in place (same type, same position), so `inner` — and with it the already-attached Yorkie `Document` holding A's content and A's un-pushed change log — is NOT remounted. But `DurableYorkieProvider` receives `userId={String(person.id)}` (line 356), and its `store` useMemo is keyed on `[userId]` (durable-yorkie-provider.tsx), so a fresh `WafflebaseDocStore({ userId: B })` is created. Every subsequent `saveSnapshot` writes `userId: this.userId` (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:629) — i.e. B — for a document whose content is A's. `listArchives`/`loadArchive`/`storedDocumentIds` all filter on `row.userId === this.userId`, so B's `OfflineRuntime` would enumerate that row, and on a `LocalChangesDropped` `remove()` archives it with `userId: header?.userId ?? this.userId` = B — after which B's "Save a copy" recovery materializes A's document content as a new server-side document B owns. The Yorkie auth webhook gates the server attach but not the local store write. I could not confirm the SDK's write ordering on re-attach (whether it snapshots before the webhook answers), which is why confidence is low; the store-scope rebinding itself is directly visible in the code. Attacker/exploit path: shared workstation, victim leaves a document open in one tab, next person signs in from another tab.

samples.summary: The share-link PDF route mounts CollabDocumentProvider outside NonDurableScope, so the positional share-link durability gate does not cover it
samples.evidence: `SharedDocumentInner` returns `<SharedPdfLayout .../>` at shared-document.tsx:969 — an EARLY RETURN that happens before the `<NonDurableScope>` wrapper added at line 1017. `SharedPdfLayout` (line 753) mounts its own `YorkieProvider` and then `PdfCollabProvider`, which renders `CollabDocumentProvider` (app/files/pdf-collab.tsx:200). `useDurabilityPermitted()` therefore answers its default `true` (use-durable-document.ts:61) on that subtree. Today the route is saved only by the unrelated `isExcluded(docKey)` rule (`docKey.startsWith('pdf-')`, use-durable-document.ts:40-42), which the design states is temporary: docs/design/offline-local-persistence.md says PDF is "excluded until it has a chip". The moment that exclusion is lifted, a signed-in visitor on somebody else's share link gets the durable branch on this route — their own `wb:{salt}:{userId}:pdf-<id>` client authenticating with `fetchYorkieToken` (their personal token) rather than the share token whose role and expiry the auth webhook validates, and the shared document's comment content written to a disk the link's revocation cannot reach. That is precisely the bypass `NonDurableScope` was added to close, and the gate reads as covering the whole share route when it does not. `shared-document-durability.test.tsx` only exercises `resolved.type: 'sheet'`, so no test covers the pdf branch.

samples.summary: An expired session (401) erases no locally stored document content, so full document text can remain on a shared device for up to thirty days
samples.evidence: `fetchWithAuth`'s 401 arm now passes `eraseLocalData: "none"`, and `logout()` only calls `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout()` when `eraseLocalData !== 'none' && res?.ok`. A session that expires — by far the commonest way a session ends on a shared/borrowed machine, and the case the whole per-device opt-in exists for — therefore leaves every live IndexedDB entry (snapshot + un-pushed change log) and every archive on that disk. `localStorage` salts likewise survive (durable-session.ts:145, thirty days). The app's own readers are userId-scoped (`listArchives`/`loadArchive`/`storedDocumentIds`), but anyone with devtools on that browser profile reads IndexedDB directly, and durable-session.ts:120-128 concedes "no client-side store can" defend against that. The compensating controls are the thirty-day sweep and the next session's reconcile, both of which require somebody to sign in again on that device. This is an explicit, reasoned trade-off in docs/design/offline-local-persistence.md § Turning it on (avoiding destruction of unsent work), so it is a risk acceptance rather than an oversight — flagged so the data-retention exposure on the stated shared-device threat model is confirmed rather than inherited.

samples.summary: randomSecret() falls back to Math.random() for the client-key salt, which would make the key derivable — the exact property the salt exists to provide
samples.evidence: `randomSecret()` (durable-session.ts:244-257) uses `crypto.getRandomValues` when available and otherwise fills the 8 bytes from `Math.floor(Math.random() * 256)`. The salt's entire purpose, stated at durable-session.ts:80-104, is that Yorkie authorizes `ActivateClient`/`DeactivateClient` on token validity alone, so a *derivable* client key lets any workspace peer holding a valid token take over or repeatedly deactivate another member's per-document client. `Math.random()` is not a CSPRNG and its state is recoverable from a handful of outputs, so on that branch the key stops being unguessable. The inline comment argues the branch is unreachable because `navigator.locks` and `crypto` are both secure-context APIs, and `supportsDurableSession()` does gate on `navigator.locks` — that reasoning is probably correct in practice (which is why this is minor), but the safe failure here is to refuse durability rather than to mint a weak salt, since the module already fails closed everywhere else for exactly this asymmetry.

samples.summary: Thrown store errors embed the full SDK store key, which contains the per-document device salt, and reach console/Sentry breadcrumbs that the capability-token scrubber does not cover
samples.evidence: `refuseIfEvicted` (line 753) and `refuseIfDisabled` (line ~520) build DOMException messages containing `docKey`, which on the durable path is the SDK's scoped key `apiKey/wb:{deviceSecret}:{userId}:{docKey}/{docKey}` — i.e. the salt in clear. Those errors propagate to the SDK and to `console.warn` sites in offline-runtime.tsx and durable-yorkie-provider.tsx. `@sentry/browser` captures console output as breadcrumbs by default, and `scrubCapabilityTokens` (src/sentry.ts:96-146) only rewrites `event.request.url`, `event.transaction`, and breadcrumb `data.url/from/to` — it does not touch breadcrumb or exception *message* text. The salt is the one ingredient of the client key a workspace peer cannot otherwise obtain, so exporting it to a third-party error tracker widens who can derive and deactivate that client row. The design already accepts that an operator can read the key from a Yorkie client row (durable-session.ts:93-100), which bounds the impact; confidence is low because I did not confirm which of these throws actually reaches a logged Sentry event.

samples.summary: isOfflineWritePermitted fails open when localStorage reads throw, so a tab other than the one that signed out can keep writing an erased account's documents back to disk
samples.evidence: `isOfflineWritePermitted` (line 208) checks the in-memory `erased` set first, then `deniedIds()`. `deniedIds()` (line 150-170) returns `[]` when `localStorage.getItem` throws, so the function returns `true` — permitted. The in-memory set only covers the JS realm that performed the sign-out, which is exactly the realm the cross-tab `localStorage` mirror was added to get past (see the comment at lines 120-143). In a second tab where storage access is refused (Safari private mode, blocked third-party storage), the still-mounted durable client keeps appending, the SDK repairs a failed append with a fresh snapshot, and the whole document returns to a disk the sign-out just cleared with nothing scheduled to remove it — the failure mode the comment describes, reached through the storage-error path instead. The module's own doc comment concedes the "a browser that refuses storage has no IndexedDB either" premise is "not a rule" (offline-local-persistence.md § Turning it on says the same), so relying on it here is inconsistent with that. Failing closed (deny when the answer cannot be read) costs a refused write the store already reports; failing open costs the feature's primary privacy control.

verdict.reason: The exploit depends on DurableYorkieProvider being reconciled in place with userId=B while `inner`'s attached document stays mounted. That render cannot commit. On the render where `person` flips A→B, `subject` (collab-document-provider.tsx:256) changes, and useDurableDocument's own subject includes userId (use-durable-document.ts:186) so `answered` is false (:232) and `settled = !eligible || answered` is false (:254) for any previously-durable document. Therefore `ready` is false (collab-document-provider.tsx:268), `held.current` is not updated (:269), and the gate at :333-335 returns null — unmounting DurabilityLapseScope, DurableYorkieProvider and the DocumentProvider/`inner` with A's document, together with A's store, before any B-scoped store exists. The B-scoped store is only created on the later render that mounts a fresh DurableYorkieProvider with clientKey `wb:…:B:docKey`. The alternate exit is also safe: if B is ineligible, `decided.durable` is false and :351 renders bare `inner` where DurableYorkieProvider was — a different element type at the same slot, so React unmounts that subtree as well. `person` cannot change without changing `subject` (:211-216), and `decided` is undefined whenever held.subject !== subject (:283-286), so userId can never drift under a held durable decision. The secondary archive step is independently guarded: remove() writes `userId: header?.userId ?? this.userId` (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:838), preferring the header written by the owning store, and rows are keyed by `apiKey/clientKey/docKey` whose client key embeds the owner (:1315-1317). Behaviour is corroborated by collab-document-provider-durable.test.tsx:173-199.

verdict.reason: The structural claim is accurate — SharedPdfLayout (shared-document.tsx:968-981, 753-793) is an early return above the NonDurableScope wrapper at shared-document.tsx:1017, and PdfCollabProvider does mount CollabDocumentProvider (pdf-collab.tsx:200-201). But the security consequence is already blocked on the enforced path. The sole production mount of DurableYorkieProvider is collab-document-provider.tsx:349-372, gated on decided.durable && decided.clientKey; those derive only from useDurableDocument, whose eligibility AND-chain includes !isExcluded(docKey) (use-durable-document.ts:127-132) with isExcluded returning true for every 'pdf-' key (use-durable-document.ts:40-42), and clientKey is undefined unless durable (use-durable-document.ts:249). The pdf share subtree mounts exactly one document, keyed pdf-<id>, so no personal-token durable client and no IndexedDB write is reachable there irrespective of the missing positional scope. acquireDurableSession/durableClientKey have no other production caller, so there is no alternate path. The only live effect of the missing scope on this route is mayPersist/identified render timing (collab-document-provider.tsx:223-224), which is UX/correctness, not authorization. The described exploit requires a future edit removing the pdf exclusion, so it is defense-in-depth hardening rather than a present vulnerability under the Security rubric.
